ideas.headline: 2026-11-19 (morning, NY): Hunterbrook Capital said it is betting against AMD (a short position) and published a report claiming a blacklisted Chinese server maker, IEIT Systems, kept getting newer AMD firmware. AMD fell as much as about 10% during the day and is now about 6.5% below the S&P 500.
ideas.why_not_priced_in: The report has gaps: Hunterbrook admits it could not find out how IEIT got the firmware or whether AMD holds export licenses, and no rule-breaking has been proven. No regulator has opened an investigation. Firmware updates that reach a blacklisted company through other server makers would mean little to AMD's big data-center and AI chip business, even in the worst case. The drop did not come from earnings or a forecast change; it was one short-seller's claim. The stock has already climbed back from about $477 at its low to about $497, so it is no longer falling fast. AMD normally swings a lot each day and trades billions of dollars a day. Risk: AMD has not yet replied, and a government export-control probe would change the picture.
ideas.plain_reason: A short-seller's unproven China claim hit AMD, but its main chip business is unchanged.

ideas.headline: 2026-11-19 16:53 UTC (CNBC): AMD falls on short-seller report of alleged China exposure; Hunterbrook says AMD firmware showed up at blacklisted IEIT Systems.
ideas.why_not_priced_in: The ~8% drop vs SPY comes from a short-seller's report that says itself it does not prove AMD broke export laws. It shows no lost sales, profit problem, guidance cut or official probe. AMD reported on Nov 3 and is not due again until about early February. This is the kind of thin-evidence short report about a big profitable company that bounced back in our tests. Risk: about 22% of AMD's sales come from China, so a real U.S. export-control investigation would change the picture.
ideas.plain_reason: A short seller's claims, with no proof of wrongdoing, scared investors out of a strong company.
